transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-08
Start time: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Jonah Patel (Redwood Eng Ops), Priya Nair (AtlasGrid - ML), Evan Brooks (AtlasGrid - Backend), Samir Rao (AtlasGrid - PM)
Links shared: https://redwood.com/poc/atlasgrid-runbook, https://github.com/atlasgrid/poc-repros (note: repo is private)

Summary (auto): quick triage of two intermittent failures seen in the pilot: 1) structured-output schema drift on function-calling responses, 2) KV cache "liveness" causing stale data to be served. Discussed SDK hook points and proposed fallbacks, agreed on repro bundle and next steps for a short Dedicated-run to verify fixes.

[00:00] Maya: ok hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. we should have about 50 minutes, i wanted to focus first on the two items you flagged in the issue tracker, priya, is that right?
[00:12] Priya: yeah thanks maya, yep the big ones are the function-calling responses sometimes coming back with missing fields and also the "lookup is stale" issue where we see old location names. it's intermittent, maybe 1-2% of requests at peak.
[00:23] Diego: quick clarifying q — when you say missing fields, is that schema-level or just nulls? like the structured JSON keys are absent or the values are null?
[00:31] Priya: keys absent mostly, so when our parser expects topology.geo.coordinates we get just a string or sometimes nothing, and that breaks our downstream pipeline.
[00:42] Evan: and on the KV cache side we think it's related to session affinity plus a long TTL in the SDK. sometimes the node serving the request hasn't pulled the latest write.
[00:53] Diego: okay that helps. for the function-calling path we're using the SDK wrapper for the runtime's function invocation, which does two things: it maps tool outputs to your schema and also applies a post-processor that can coerce or drop keys. i've seen cases where, under backpressure, the post-processor path can run on a slightly older model variant — so you get schema drift.
[01:15] Priya: are you saying model variant mismatches can change the json shape? that seems worrying.
[01:19] Diego: yeah, it's subtle: if the request falls back to a smaller quantized variant (we do that for cost-latency tradeoffs), some of the llm's function-calling heuristics are different and that can produce slightly different structured output. we should have flagged that earlier in the rollout.
[01:34] Samir: wait so is the fallback happening automatically during your burst policy? we are on the hosted pilot tier right now.
[01:40] Jonah: correct, AtlasGrid's pilot is routed through our standard routing policy — we do soft fallbacks to a compatible variant when the primary is at capacity. usually it's harmless but with strict JSON schemas it can surface.
[01:52] Priya: ok that explains the missing keys, that tracks with the timestamps we collected. what's the recommended mitigation?
[01:58] Diego: couple options: 1) pin the model version for critical routes (we can add a route-level pin in the console), 2) adjust fallback policy to only return text for non-critical calls, or 3) implement a resilient post-processor that can fill defaults. i can push a sample fallback handler to the repo today.
[02:16] Priya: option 1 or 3 would be best. pinning is fine for small volumes; but we can't afford to block the whole route forever. the resilient post-processor sounds pragmatic.
[02:25] Diego: i'll add it. sample behavior: validate against the JSON schema and if a key is missing, call the SDK's quick-hydrate function which issues a lightweight completion to fill the value, or mark the record for async enrichment.
[02:38] Evan: what's the latency impact of that quick-hydrate call? if it's synchronous it could worsen P95.
[02:43] Diego: good point — the handler will be async by default. sync only for critical single-record flows. also we can set a short timeout like 200-300ms.
[02:52] Priya: perfect. second issue — KV cache liveness. our traces show nodes serving reads that are 10-20m older than the write.
[03:01] Jonah: ok so a few moving parts: the SDK maintains a local prefix cache (we call it KV cache but i know that's overloaded), the runtime also has a shared KV store with eventual consistency across pods, and there is a short window where pod failover + sticky session can return stale data.
[03:17] Evan: we're on SDK v0.9.2 and we left default cache_ttl at 30m because it helped reduce token cost.
[03:24] Diego: that's long for dynamic user data. recommend moving TTL to 60s-120s for hotspots and adding a write-through invalidation hook. we have an SDK callback for onWriteInvalidate that can nudge other nodes. i'll attach code.
[03:38] Priya: we noticed the SDK docs referenced onWriteInvalidate but the sample didn't show multi-region. does that flow to VPC/private deployments?
[03:45] Maya: yes the callback is available across hosted and dedicated. for private/VPC there are extra networking hops but the semantics are the same — but you'll want to enable KMS and ensure your audit logs are preserved.
[03:55] Samir: could the quanti-quantization (quant-ization) or kernel selection have an effect on KV behavior?
[04:02] Diego: not directly; quantization affects tokenization/latency and occasional output fidelity, not the cache. the liveness is operational. root cause is the sticky affinity to pod that hasn't seen the write.
[04:14] Evan: ok what's the repro plan so we can generate a reliable test?
[04:18] Maya: priya will give a small anonymized session set, evan will run a 30-minute load with a mixture of reads/writes hitting the same keys, and diego will provide an instrumentation patch that logs cache hits/misses + node id header. then we'll converge on a TTL that keeps tail latency acceptable.
[04:33] Priya: timeline? we can get the sample data over today.
[04:36] Evan: i can run the load Tuesday morning our time and share traces.
[04:40] Diego: i'll try to get the patch into the repro repo by EOD.
[04:44] Samir: fantastic. one other small item — our integration tests found that the SDK's error objects sometimes differ between python and node wrappers, which makes our orchestration brittle.
[04:54] Maya: yes we've seen slight differences historically; we're converging on a unified error contract this quarter. diego, can you add a mapping table to the repo and a small compatibility shim?
[05:03] Diego: yeah will do. i'll add a migration doc and example shim for node->python parity.
[05:09] Priya: do you have any guidance for schema validation in the SDK? we use a JSON schema verifier but it chokes with trailing commas in some function-calls.
[05:18] Diego: trailing commas are a common parsing nuisance — our post-processor runs a lenient JSON parser first, then normalizes. i'll include the normalization rules in the snippet. also we can enable a lint-mode in the console for the route which will block responses that don't validate (helpful in canary).
[05:33] Priya: that lint-mode would be excellent for our canary runs.
[05:36] Maya: ok to recap next steps — diego adds fallback handler, invalidation hook, error mapping and normalization snippets; priya/evan provide data and run load; maya will send security docs and pricing. we'll reconvene after the load results.
[05:49] Samir: any blockers on pilot expansion? we wanted to try a small Dedicated run to verify tail latency fixes.
[05:55] Maya: we can schedule a short Dedicated burst for testing next week; i'll add pricing and the commit options in the email.
[06:01] Priya: perfect, thanks everyone.

Meeting end notes:
- Artifacts: repro bundle (private repo), runbook link above, diego's upcoming branch with instrumentation.
- Agreed: try TTL 60s on hotspot keys, add async quick-hydrate for missing fields, and run a 30-minute load test capturing traces and node ids.
